```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.2, fig.align = "center")
```

Bolker gives a one-paragraph footnote explaining where the $2k$ in
$\text{AIC} = -2\log\mathcal{L} + 2k$ comes from (Section 6.6.2;
printed p. 210 in the published book, p. 277 in the free draft). The
footnote is hard to follow, and it has a gap: it does one Taylor
expansion, which yields $k/2$, then drops a factor of $\tfrac12$ to
reach $k$. The full argument
needs **two** expansions, each contributing $k/2$.

These notes do the derivation in full:

1. what AIC is trying to estimate (Section 1);
2. a one-parameter example where every step can be done with ordinary
   algebra and the answer comes out exact (Section 2);
3. the matrix tools needed for $k$ parameters (Section 3);
4. the two halves of the penalty with matrices (Sections 4 and 5);
5. a simulation check (Section 6), what can break (Section 7), and
   Bolker's footnote line by line (Section 8).

Section 2 is the one worth showing students. Sections 3 to 5 are the
same argument with matrices and are mostly for the instructor.

# 1. What AIC is trying to estimate

## Notation

Bolker's footnote uses $x$ for both the data and the parameters, which
is most of why it's hard to read. Here:

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:--------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|
| $f$ | the true process that generates data (unknown) |
| $g(y \mid \theta)$ | the candidate model: probability of data $y$ given parameters $\theta$ |
| $k$ | number of parameters; $\theta$ is a column vector of length $k$ |
| $y$ | the observed dataset, used to fit the model |
| $y^*$ | an imaginary **new** dataset, same size, drawn independently from $f$ |
| $\text{NLL}_y(\theta)$ | negative log-likelihood computed from dataset $y$: $-\log g(y \mid \theta)$ |
| $\hat\theta$ | the MLE from the observed data; it minimizes $\text{NLL}_y(\theta)$ |
| $\theta_0$ | the "best" parameter value for this model (defined below) |

The subscript on NLL marks which dataset it's computed from, following
the course convention of writing a likelihood as a function of the
parameter alone.

## Kullback-Leibler distance, minus the part we can't compute

The K-L distance from the truth $f$ to the model at parameter $\theta$
is the expected log ratio of their predictions, averaged over the true
distribution of the data:
$$D(\theta) = E_f\!\left[\log \frac{f(y^*)}{g(y^* \mid \theta)}\right]
 = \underbrace{E_f[\log f(y^*)]}_{\text{same for every model}}
 \;+\; E_f[-\log g(y^* \mid \theta)].$$
The first term involves only the truth, so it's the same constant for
every candidate model and drops out of any comparison. What's left is
the expected NLL on new data:
$$Q(\theta) = E_{y^*}\big[\text{NLL}_{y^*}(\theta)\big].$$
Smaller $Q$ means closer to the truth. Define $\theta_0$ as the value
that minimizes $Q$: the best this model family can do. If the model
family contains the truth, $\theta_0$ is the true parameter value;
otherwise it's the closest approximation (sometimes called the
"pseudo-true" value). It is not an MLE. It's a fixed, unknown target,
just like a true parameter value.

## The target, and why the obvious estimate is biased

We never get to use $\theta_0$. We use $\hat\theta$, fitted from $y$.
So the fair measure of a fitted model is how well $\hat\theta$ predicts
**new** data, averaged over the datasets we might have collected:
$$T = E_y\big[\,Q(\hat\theta)\,\big]
 = E_y\Big[\,E_{y^*}\big[\text{NLL}_{y^*}(\hat\theta)\big]\Big].$$
Two expectations appear because two things are random: the data used
to fit ($y$, which determines $\hat\theta$), and the data used to judge
($y^*$). Bolker's "E[E[...]]" is this double expectation.

The obvious estimate of $T$ is the observed minimum, $\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)$.
But it uses the same data twice, once to choose $\hat\theta$ and once
to score it. $\hat\theta$ was chosen to make $\text{NLL}_y$ as small as
possible, so it fits $y$ better than it will fit $y^*$, and
$\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)$ is too small on average. The more parameters,
the more freedom to fit noise in $y$, and the larger this optimism.

**The whole result:** the average optimism is about $k$.
$$T \approx E_y\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)\big] + k
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
2T \approx E\big[\underbrace{2\,\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta) + 2k}_{\text{AIC}}\big].$$
Multiplying by 2 just puts things on the deviance scale. So AIC is an
(approximately unbiased) estimate of twice the expected out-of-sample
NLL, which is the model-dependent part of the expected K-L distance.

The bridge between the observed $\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)$ and the
target $Q(\hat\theta)$ goes through $\theta_0$, in two steps:
$$\underbrace{Q(\hat\theta) - Q(\theta_0)}_{\text{Half 1: cost of using }\hat\theta}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\underbrace{Q(\theta_0) - \text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)}_{\text{Half 2: optimism of the in-sample fit}}.$$
Each averages about $k/2$.

# 2. Warm-up: one parameter, no matrices, exact answer

Suppose we measure snout-vent length (mm) of $n = 10$ lizards, each
$y_i \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, and pretend $\sigma = 4$ is
known (say, from a much larger study), so $k = 1$. The truth is
$\mu_0 = 60$.

## The observed NLL

$$\text{NLL}_y(\mu) = n\log\big(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\big) +
 \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \mu)^2.$$
The sum of squares splits around the sample mean $\bar y$. Add and
subtract $\bar y$ inside the square, then expand $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$
with $a = y_i - \bar y$ and $b = \bar y - \mu$:
$$\sum (y_i - \mu)^2 = \sum \big[(y_i - \bar y) + (\bar y - \mu)\big]^2
 = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2 + 2\sum (y_i - \bar y)(\bar y - \mu) + \sum (\bar y - \mu)^2.$$
The last term has no $i$ in it, so summing it $n$ times gives
$n(\bar y - \mu)^2$. In the middle (cross) term, $(\bar y - \mu)$ also
doesn't depend on $i$, so it factors out of the sum:
$$2\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar y)(\bar y - \mu) = 2(\bar y - \mu)\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar y).$$
The remaining sum is zero, because deviations from the mean always
cancel:
$$\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar y) = \sum_{i=1}^n y_i - n\bar y = n\bar y - n\bar y = 0,$$
using $\sum y_i = n\bar y$ (the definition of the mean). So the cross
term drops out, leaving
$$\sum (y_i - \mu)^2 = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2 + n(\bar y - \mu)^2.$$
Substituting into the NLL:
$$\text{NLL}_y(\mu) = C + \frac{S}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{n(\bar y - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2},
\qquad C = n\log\big(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}\big),\; S = \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2.$$
This is a parabola in $\mu$ with its minimum at $\hat\mu = \bar y$.

## The expected NLL on new data

For one new observation, $E[(y_i^* - \mu)^2] = \text{Var}(y_i^*) +
(E[y_i^*] - \mu)^2 = \sigma^2 + (\mu_0 - \mu)^2$. Summing over $n$
observations:
$$Q(\mu) = C + \frac{n\big[\sigma^2 + (\mu - \mu_0)^2\big]}{2\sigma^2}
 = C + \frac{n}{2} + \frac{n(\mu - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma^2}.$$
Another parabola, with the same curvature, but its minimum is at the
truth, $\mu_0$.

## Half 1: the cost of using $\hat\mu$ instead of $\mu_0$

Plug $\hat\mu = \bar y$ into $Q$ and subtract $Q(\mu_0)$:
$$Q(\hat\mu) - Q(\mu_0) = \frac{n(\bar y - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma^2}
 = \frac12 \left(\frac{\bar y - \mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\right)^2 = \frac12 Z^2,$$
where $Z$ is a standard normal (since $\bar y \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_0, \sigma^2/n)$).
$E[Z^2] = \text{Var}(Z) = 1$, so this half averages $\tfrac12$.

## Half 2: the optimism of the in-sample fit

Evaluate the observed NLL at the truth and at the MLE:
$$\text{NLL}_y(\mu_0) - \text{NLL}_y(\hat\mu) = \frac{n(\bar y - \mu_0)^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac12 Z^2.$$
The same quantity again, averaging $\tfrac12$. (This is also half the
likelihood ratio statistic, which Wilks' theorem says is $\chi^2_1$
with mean 1.) To connect it to $Q(\mu_0)$, take the expectation of
$\text{NLL}_y(\mu_0)$ directly: $\mu_0$ is a fixed number, so this is
just $Q(\mu_0)$, since $y$ and $y^*$ have the same distribution.
Therefore
$$E\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\mu)\big] = Q(\mu_0) - \tfrac12.$$

## Putting them together

$$T = E[Q(\hat\mu)] = Q(\mu_0) + \tfrac12
 = E\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\mu)\big] + \tfrac12 + \tfrac12
 = E\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\mu)\big] + 1.$$
With $k = 1$ the optimism is 1, and $2 \times 1 = 2k$. In this example
there's no approximation anywhere: both NLL curves are parabolas, so the
Taylor expansions in Sections 4 and 5 are exact.

```{r warmup-sim}
n_liz <- 10
sigma <- 4
mu0 <- 60
nll_obs <- function(mu, y) -sum(dnorm(y, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
q_fun <- function(mu) n_liz * log(sigma * sqrt(2 * pi)) +
  n_liz / 2 + n_liz * (mu - mu0)^2 / (2 * sigma^2)

set.seed(143)
y_liz <- rnorm(n_liz, mu0, sigma)
mu_hat <- mean(y_liz)
```

```{r fig-warmup, fig.height=3.6}
mu_grid <- seq(56, 64, length.out = 400)
nll_curve <- sapply(mu_grid, nll_obs, y = y_liz)
q_curve <- q_fun(mu_grid)

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 0.5))
plot(mu_grid, q_curve, type = "l", lwd = 2, lty = 2,
     ylim = range(c(nll_curve, q_curve, 27, 30)),
     xlab = "mu (mean snout-vent length, mm)", ylab = "NLL")
lines(mu_grid, nll_curve, lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(mu0, mu_hat), lty = 3, col = "grey50")
points(c(mu0, mu_hat, mu_hat, mu0),
       c(q_fun(mu0), q_fun(mu_hat), nll_obs(mu_hat, y_liz), nll_obs(mu0, y_liz)),
       pch = c(1, 16, 16, 1), cex = 1.2)
arrows(mu_hat + 0.15, q_fun(mu0), mu_hat + 0.15, q_fun(mu_hat), length = 0.06, code = 3)
segments(mu0, q_fun(mu0), mu_hat + 0.15, q_fun(mu0), lty = 3)
arrows(mu0 - 0.15, nll_obs(mu_hat, y_liz), mu0 - 0.15, nll_obs(mu0, y_liz),
       length = 0.06, code = 3)
segments(mu0 - 0.15, nll_obs(mu_hat, y_liz), mu_hat, nll_obs(mu_hat, y_liz), lty = 3)
text(mu_hat + 0.2, mean(c(q_fun(mu0), q_fun(mu_hat))), "Half 1", pos = 4, cex = 0.8)
text(mu0 - 0.2, mean(c(nll_obs(mu_hat, y_liz), nll_obs(mu0, y_liz))), "Half 2",
     pos = 2, cex = 0.8)
mtext(c("true mu", "MLE"), side = 3, at = c(mu0, mu_hat), line = 0, cex = 0.75)
legend("top", c("Q (expected NLL, new data)", "observed NLL"), lty = c(2, 1),
       lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.75, inset = 0.03)
```

The figure shows one simulated sample ($\bar y$ = `r round(mu_hat, 2)`).
The dashed curve $Q$ is centered on the truth; the solid observed
curve is centered on the MLE. Half 1 is how far up $Q$'s wall the MLE
sits. Half 2 is how far up the observed curve's wall the truth sits. In
this one-parameter normal case they're the same height, $\tfrac12 Z^2$.

This sample was chosen so the two curves nearly meet at $\mu_0$, which
makes both halves easy to see. Nothing forces that. The figure below
draws the observed curve for 12 more simulated samples around the same
$Q$.

```{r fig-warmup-many, fig.height=3.6}
set.seed(746)
n_curves <- 12
y_many <- matrix(rnorm(n_curves * n_liz, mu0, sigma), ncol = n_curves)
nll_many <- apply(y_many, 2, function(y) sapply(mu_grid, nll_obs, y = y))
mu_hat_many <- colMeans(y_many)

y_big <- matrix(rnorm(20000 * n_liz, mu0, sigma), ncol = 20000)
gap_mu0 <- colSums((y_big - mu0)^2) / (2 * sigma^2) - n_liz / 2
nll_avg <- sapply(mu_grid, function(m) mean(colSums((y_big - m)^2)) / (2 * sigma^2)) +
  n_liz * log(sigma * sqrt(2 * pi))

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 0.5))
matplot(mu_grid, nll_many, type = "l", lty = 1, lwd = 1, col = "grey60",
        ylim = range(nll_many) + c(0, 8),
        xlab = "mu (mean snout-vent length, mm)", ylab = "NLL")
points(mu_hat_many, apply(y_many, 2, function(y) nll_obs(mean(y), y)),
       pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = "grey40")
points(rep(mu0, n_curves), apply(y_many, 2, nll_obs, mu = mu0), pch = 1, cex = 0.8)
lines(mu_grid, q_curve, lwd = 2.5, lty = 2)
abline(v = mu0, lty = 3, col = "grey50")
mtext("true mu", side = 3, at = mu0, line = 0, cex = 0.75)
legend("top", c("Q (same for every sample)", "observed NLL, 12 samples",
                "MLE of each sample", "each curve at true mu"),
       lty = c(2, 1, NA, NA), lwd = c(2.5, 1, NA, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 16, 1),
       col = c("black", "grey60", "grey40", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.7,
       inset = 0.02)
```

What stays put and what moves:

- **$Q$ doesn't depend on the data.** It's the same dashed curve for
  every sample.
- **Each observed curve has the same shape as $Q$** (curvature
  $n/\sigma^2$ in this example), but its position is random. It slides
  sideways with $\bar y$; that sideways shift is what both halves
  measure. It also slides up and down, because the height at $\mu_0$
  depends on $\sum (y_i - \mu_0)^2$.
- **The vertical gap at $\mu_0$ is large.** It equals
  $\big[\sum (y_i - \mu_0)^2/\sigma^2 - n\big]/2 = (\chi^2_n - n)/2$,
  with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sqrt{n/2} \approx$
  `r round(sqrt(n_liz / 2), 1)` NLL units (`r round(sd(gap_mu0), 2)` in
  20,000 simulated samples). That's much larger than either half,
  which averages 0.5.
- **On average the observed curves sit on $Q$.** Averaging the observed
  NLL over all those simulated samples at each $\mu$ reproduces $Q$
  (largest difference along the curve:
  `r signif(max(abs(nll_avg - q_curve)), 1)`). This is the definition
  of $Q$, and it's why Half 2 only needs the expectation
  $E_y[\text{NLL}_y(\mu_0)] = Q(\mu_0)$, never a match in any single
  sample.

# 3. Matrix tools for $k$ parameters

With $k$ parameters, the slopes and curvatures of Section 2 become a
vector and a matrix. Everything below treats vectors as columns, and
$^T$ means transpose (turn a column into a row).

## Gradient and Hessian

For a function $h(\theta)$ of $\theta = (\theta_1, \dots, \theta_k)^T$:

- The **gradient** $\nabla h$ is the column of first partial
  derivatives, $(\partial h/\partial\theta_1, \dots, \partial h/\partial\theta_k)^T$.
  At a minimum, every entry is zero.
- The **Hessian** $H$ is the $k \times k$ matrix of second partial
  derivatives, $H_{ij} = \partial^2 h / \partial\theta_i\,\partial\theta_j$.
  It's symmetric ($H_{ij} = H_{ji}$). Diagonal entries are the curvature
  along each parameter axis; off-diagonal entries describe how the
  surface twists (how the slope in one parameter changes as another
  changes).

## Quadratic forms

For a vector $\Delta$ and a symmetric matrix $A$, the **quadratic form**
$\Delta^T A \Delta$ is a single number:
$$\Delta^T A \Delta = \sum_{i=1}^k \sum_{j=1}^k \Delta_i\, A_{ij}\, \Delta_j.$$
For $k = 2$, written out:
$$\Delta^T A \Delta = A_{11}\Delta_1^2 + 2A_{12}\Delta_1\Delta_2 + A_{22}\Delta_2^2.$$
With $k = 1$ it's $A\Delta^2$, which is what appeared in Section 2.

## Taylor expansion in several variables

The one-variable second-order expansion
$h(\theta_0 + \Delta) \approx h(\theta_0) + h'(\theta_0)\Delta + \tfrac12 h''(\theta_0)\Delta^2$
becomes
$$h(\theta_0 + \Delta) \approx h(\theta_0) + \nabla h(\theta_0)^T \Delta
 + \tfrac12\, \Delta^T H(\theta_0)\, \Delta.$$
The middle term, $\nabla h^T \Delta = \sum_i (\partial h/\partial\theta_i)\Delta_i$,
is a single number (a row times a column). If $\theta_0$ is a minimum,
it's zero.

## Inner and outer products

For a column vector $\Delta$ there are two different products with
itself, and the difference matters for one of Bolker's errors:

- **Inner product** $\Delta^T\Delta$ (row times column): a single
  number, $\sum_i \Delta_i^2$.
- **Outer product** $\Delta\Delta^T$ (column times row): a $k\times k$
  matrix whose $(i, j)$ entry is $\Delta_i\Delta_j$.

If $\Delta = \hat\theta - \theta_0$ and $E[\Delta] \approx 0$, the
expected outer product is the **variance-covariance matrix** of the
estimates:
$$\Sigma = E[\Delta\Delta^T], \qquad
\Sigma_{ii} = E[\Delta_i^2] = \text{Var}(\hat\theta_i), \qquad
\Sigma_{ij} = E[\Delta_i\Delta_j] = \text{Cov}(\hat\theta_i, \hat\theta_j).$$
The expected inner product is a single number, the sum of the
variances, so it can't be $\Sigma$.

## Trace, and the trace trick

The **trace** of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal:
$\text{tr}(M) = \sum_i M_{ii}$. Two facts:

- **Trace of a product.** The $i$-th diagonal entry of $AB$ is
  $\sum_j A_{ij}B_{ji}$, so $\text{tr}(AB) = \sum_i\sum_j A_{ij}B_{ji}$.
  Swapping the names of $i$ and $j$ shows $\text{tr}(AB) = \text{tr}(BA)$.
- **Trace of the identity.** The $k\times k$ identity matrix $I_k$ has
  ones on the diagonal, so $\text{tr}(I_k) = k$. **This is where the $k$
  in AIC comes from.**

The **trace trick** turns the expectation of a quadratic form into a
trace. Start from the double sum and regroup:
$$\Delta^T A \Delta = \sum_i\sum_j A_{ij}\,\Delta_j\Delta_i
 = \sum_i\sum_j A_{ij}\,(\Delta\Delta^T)_{ji}
 = \text{tr}\big(A\,\Delta\Delta^T\big).$$
The last step is the trace-of-a-product formula with $B = \Delta\Delta^T$.
Expectation is linear and $A$ is fixed, so it passes inside the sums:
$$\boxed{\;E\big[\Delta^T A \Delta\big] = \text{tr}\big(A\,E[\Delta\Delta^T]\big) = \text{tr}(A\,\Sigma).\;}$$
(This holds for any random vector. If $E[\Delta] = b \ne 0$, then
$E[\Delta\Delta^T] = \Sigma + bb^T$, but for an MLE the bias $b$ is small
in large samples and is ignored here.)

```{r trace-check}
set.seed(746)
a_mat <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 3), 2)
sigma_mat <- matrix(c(0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2), 2)
delta <- matrix(rnorm(2e5 * 2), ncol = 2) %*% chol(sigma_mat)
qf_mean <- mean(rowSums((delta %*% a_mat) * delta))
tr_val <- sum(diag(a_mat %*% sigma_mat))
```

**Check with numbers.** Let $A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$
and $\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} 0.5 & 0.1 \\ 0.1 & 0.2\end{pmatrix}$. Then
$$\text{tr}(A\Sigma) = (2)(0.5) + (1)(0.1) + (1)(0.1) + (3)(0.2) = 1.8.$$
Writing out the $k = 2$ quadratic form instead:
$E[2\Delta_1^2 + 2\Delta_1\Delta_2 + 3\Delta_2^2] = 2(0.5) + 2(0.1) + 3(0.2) = 1.8$,
the same thing. Averaging $\Delta^T A\Delta$ over 200,000 simulated
normal vectors with covariance $\Sigma$ gives `r round(qf_mean, 3)`.

## Information and the variance of the MLE

The **Fisher information matrix** for the whole dataset is the expected
Hessian of the NLL at $\theta_0$:
$$\mathcal{I} = E\big[\nabla^2\,\text{NLL}_y(\theta_0)\big],$$
the matrix version of the curvature $I$ in the likelihood theory
reference notes. Those notes showed that, when the model is correct,
$\text{Var}(\hat\theta) \approx 1/I$ for one parameter. The matrix
version is
$$\Sigma \approx \mathcal{I}^{-1},$$
where $\mathcal{I}^{-1}$ is the matrix inverse ($\mathcal{I}\,\mathcal{I}^{-1} = I_k$).
This is the variance-covariance matrix R reports as the inverse of the
Hessian from `optim(..., hessian = TRUE)`.

Sign conventions trip people up here. The Hessian of the NLL is
positive at a minimum, and its expectation is the information. The
Hessian of the **log-likelihood** is the negative of that. Bolker's $V$
is the Hessian of the log-likelihood, so his $-V^{-1} \approx \Sigma$ is
the same statement as $\mathcal{I}^{-1} \approx \Sigma$.

# 4. Half 1: the cost of using $\hat\theta$ instead of $\theta_0$

**Goal:** show $E_y[Q(\hat\theta)] \approx Q(\theta_0) + k/2$.

**Step 1: expand $Q$ around $\theta_0$.** Let $\Delta = \hat\theta - \theta_0$.
Using the multivariate Taylor expansion from Section 3,
$$Q(\hat\theta) \approx Q(\theta_0) + \nabla Q(\theta_0)^T\Delta
 + \tfrac12\,\Delta^T\,\nabla^2 Q(\theta_0)\,\Delta.$$

**Step 2: the linear term vanishes.** $\theta_0$ was defined as the
minimum of $Q$, so $\nabla Q(\theta_0) = 0$. This is where "the
likelihood is flat" is used in this half: the **expected** NLL is flat
at $\theta_0$. (The observed NLL is not flat at $\theta_0$; it's flat at
$\hat\theta$.)

**Step 3: the curvature is the information.** $Q$ is the expected
NLL, and the derivative of an expectation is the expectation of the
derivative:
$$\nabla^2 Q(\theta_0) = E\big[\nabla^2\,\text{NLL}_{y^*}(\theta_0)\big] = \mathcal{I}.$$
So
$$Q(\hat\theta) \approx Q(\theta_0) + \tfrac12\,\Delta^T\mathcal{I}\,\Delta.$$

A note on what's random. $Q(\hat\theta)$ means: take the fitted value
$\hat\theta$ from $y$, hold it fixed, and average its NLL over new
datasets $y^*$. The only thing still random is $\hat\theta$ (through
$y$), which is why only $\Delta$ is random in this expression. This
works because $y^*$ is independent of $y$.

**Step 4: average over $y$ with the trace trick.** $\mathcal{I}$ is a
fixed matrix, so
$$E_y\big[\Delta^T\mathcal{I}\,\Delta\big] = \text{tr}\big(\mathcal{I}\,\Sigma\big)
 \approx \text{tr}\big(\mathcal{I}\,\mathcal{I}^{-1}\big) = \text{tr}(I_k) = k.$$

**Result:**
$$\boxed{\;E_y\big[Q(\hat\theta)\big] \approx Q(\theta_0) + \frac{k}{2}.\;}$$
Every parameter that has to be estimated adds, on average, half a unit
of NLL on new data, regardless of whether it's a slope, an intercept,
or a variance. That independence from the parameter's units is what
the trace trick buys: $\mathcal{I}$ and $\Sigma$ both depend on
the units, but their product doesn't.

# 5. Half 2: the optimism of the in-sample fit

**Goal:** show $E_y[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)] \approx Q(\theta_0) - k/2$.

**Step 1: expand the observed NLL around $\hat\theta$, and evaluate it
at $\theta_0$.** Now $\theta_0 = \hat\theta - \Delta$, so the step away
from the expansion point is $-\Delta$:
$$\text{NLL}_y(\theta_0) \approx \text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)
 + \nabla\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)^T(-\Delta)
 + \tfrac12\,(-\Delta)^T\,\hat{\mathcal{I}}\,(-\Delta),$$
where $\hat{\mathcal{I}} = \nabla^2\,\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)$ is the
**observed** information (the Hessian R reports from `optim`).

**Step 2: the linear term vanishes.** $\hat\theta$ minimizes the
observed NLL, so $\nabla\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta) = 0$. This is the
place where "the likelihood is flat at $\hat\theta$" is the right
reason. The two minus signs in the quadratic term cancel:
$$\text{NLL}_y(\theta_0) \approx \text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta) + \tfrac12\,\Delta^T\hat{\mathcal{I}}\,\Delta.$$

**Step 3: average over $y$.** The left side: $\theta_0$ is a fixed
number, not fitted from $y$, so
$E_y[\text{NLL}_y(\theta_0)] = Q(\theta_0)$ (the observed dataset is
just one more draw from $f$, like $y^*$). The right side: in large
samples $\hat{\mathcal{I}} \approx \mathcal{I}$ (the observed curvature
is close to the expected curvature), so the trace trick gives
$$E_y\big[\Delta^T\hat{\mathcal{I}}\,\Delta\big] \approx \text{tr}(\mathcal{I}\,\Sigma) \approx k.$$

**Result:**
$$Q(\theta_0) \approx E_y\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)\big] + \frac{k}{2}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\boxed{\;E_y\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)\big] \approx Q(\theta_0) - \frac{k}{2}.\;}$$

The in-sample minimum sits, on average, $k/2$ below what even the best
possible parameter value achieves on new data. This half has a second
derivation that doesn't need the trace: $2[\text{NLL}_y(\theta_0) -
\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)]$ is the likelihood ratio statistic for testing
$\theta = \theta_0$, which by Wilks' theorem is approximately
$\chi^2_k$, with mean $k$.

## Combining the halves

$$T = E_y\big[Q(\hat\theta)\big]
 \approx Q(\theta_0) + \frac k2
 \approx \Big(E_y\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)\big] + \frac k2\Big) + \frac k2
 = E_y\big[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta)\big] + k.$$
So $\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta) + k$ is an approximately unbiased estimate
of $T$, and doubling it gives
$$\text{AIC} = 2\,\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta) + 2k = -2\log\mathcal{L}(\hat\theta) + 2k.$$
The two halves aren't double counting. They measure two different
distances: Half 1 is how far the fitted model is from the best model
when judged on new data; Half 2 is how much the fitted model flatters
itself on the data it was fitted to.

# 6. Simulation check

```{r sim-setup}
nll_pois <- function(mu, y) -sum(dpois(y, mu, log = TRUE))

# one rep: fit the first k columns of x to y; score on y and on new data y_new
aic_gap <- function(k, x, mu_true) {
  y <- rpois(length(mu_true), mu_true)
  y_new <- rpois(length(mu_true), mu_true)
  fit <- glm.fit(x[, seq_len(k), drop = FALSE], y, family = poisson())
  c(half1 = nll_pois(fitted(fit), y_new) - nll_pois(mu_true, y_new),
    half2 = nll_pois(mu_true, y) - nll_pois(fitted(fit), y))
}
```

```{r sim-run, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(746)
n_plots <- 50
k_max <- 7
reps <- 4000
x_all <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(n_plots * (k_max - 1)), n_plots))
beta_true <- c(0.5, 0.3, -0.2, rep(0, k_max - 3))
mu_true <- exp(x_all %*% beta_true)[, 1]

k_vals <- 3:k_max
gaps <- lapply(k_vals, function(k) sapply(seq_len(reps), function(i) aic_gap(k, x_all, mu_true)))
gap_means <- t(sapply(gaps, rowMeans))
gap_se <- t(sapply(gaps, function(g) apply(g, 1, sd) / sqrt(reps)))
gap_tab <- data.frame(k = k_vals, half1 = gap_means[, "half1"],
                      half2 = gap_means[, "half2"],
                      total = rowSums(gap_means))
```

To check the result outside the tidy normal case, simulate counts of
some organism in $n = 50$ plots with a Poisson log-linear model: an
intercept and two real covariates ($k = 3$ true parameters). Then fit
models with $k = 3, 4, \dots, 7$ parameters, where the extra covariates
are pure noise (their true coefficients are zero, so each fitted model
still contains the truth). For each of `r format(reps, big.mark = ",")`
simulated datasets per $k$, fit to $y$, then compute:

- **Half 1:** NLL of the fitted means on a new dataset $y^*$, minus NLL
  of the true means on $y^*$. (Using the same $y^*$ for both cancels
  most of the noise; its expectation is $Q(\hat\theta) - Q(\theta_0)$.)
- **Half 2:** NLL of the true means on $y$, minus NLL of the fitted
  means on $y$.

```{r sim-table}
knitr::kable(gap_tab, digits = 2, col.names = c("k", "Half 1", "Half 2",
             "Total (estimate of k)"), align = "c")
```

```{r fig-sim, fig.height=3.2}
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 0.5))
plot(k_vals, gap_tab$total, pch = 16, xlim = c(2.8, k_max + 0.2),
     ylim = c(0, k_max + 0.5), xlab = "Number of parameters, k",
     ylab = "Average NLL gap")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
abline(0, 0.5, lty = 3)
points(k_vals, gap_tab$half1, pch = 2)
points(k_vals, gap_tab$half2, pch = 6)
legend("topleft", c("Total (out-of-sample minus in-sample)", "Half 1", "Half 2",
                    "k", "k/2"),
       pch = c(16, 2, 6, NA, NA), lty = c(NA, NA, NA, 2, 3), bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
```

Each half tracks $k/2$ (dotted line) and the total tracks $k$ (dashed).
Monte Carlo standard errors for the halves are about
`r round(max(gap_se), 2)` or smaller. The total creeps above $k$ as $k$
grows, by more than simulation noise explains: with $n = 50$, $n/k$ is
getting small, and the large-sample approximations start to understate
the optimism (Section 7).

# 7. What the derivation assumed

Each "$\approx$" above is an assumption, and each one can fail.

- **Large $n$.** The quadratic (parabola) approximation, $E[\Delta]
  \approx 0$, and $\hat{\mathcal{I}} \approx \mathcal{I}$ all need
  reasonably large samples relative to $k$. When $n/k$ is small, the
  optimism is larger than $k$. AIC$_c$ corrects for this; its
  correction term, $2k(k+1)/(n-k-1)$, comes from doing the two halves
  without approximation for the normal linear regression model (with
  $\sigma$ estimated), so it's exact there and a reasonable patch
  elsewhere.
- **The model family contains the truth, or nearly so.** The step
  $\Sigma \approx \mathcal{I}^{-1}$ relies on the information identity
  (variance of the score equals its slope; Section 4 of the likelihood
  theory reference notes). If the model is badly wrong, the variance
  of the score, call it $K$, no longer equals $\mathcal{I}$, and the
  sandwich formula $\Sigma \approx \mathcal{I}^{-1}K\,\mathcal{I}^{-1}$
  applies instead. Then the trace becomes
  $$\text{tr}(\mathcal{I}\,\Sigma) \approx
  \text{tr}(\mathcal{I}\,\mathcal{I}^{-1}K\,\mathcal{I}^{-1})
  = \text{tr}(K\,\mathcal{I}^{-1}),$$
  which isn't $k$ in general. Using this in place of $k$ gives
  Takeuchi's information criterion (TIC). It's rarely used because
  $K$ is hard to estimate well; AIC is the version that assumes the
  candidate models are at least roughly adequate. (This is one reason
  to check goodness of fit before comparing models with AIC: a model
  that fits badly can still "win.")
- **Regular parameters.** Parameters on a boundary (a variance
  component at zero, a probability at 0 or 1) break the parabola
  approximation. Mixed and hierarchical models also make "number of
  parameters" ambiguous, which is why they need special versions (e.g.
  DIC, WAIC) later in the course.

# 8. Bolker's footnote, line by line

Using the notation above (his $x_0$ is our $\theta_0$, his $\hat{x}$ is
our $\hat\theta$, his $g(x_0)$ is our $g(y \mid \theta_0)$):

1. **Setup.** The K-L distance and dropping the $\int f \log f$
   constant: correct, and matches Section 1. Calling AIC "the expected
   value of the K-L distance" is loose: AIC estimates twice the
   expected *relative* K-L distance (the part that differs between
   models).
2. **"the true MLE $x_0$."** $\theta_0$ is not an MLE. It's the K-L-best
   parameter value, which equals the true value only when the model is
   correct.
3. **Using $x$ for both data and parameters.** The densities $g(x_0)$
   and $g(\hat x)$ are functions of the data, evaluated at a
   parameter value. The footnote never distinguishes the data used to
   fit from the data used to judge ($y$ versus $y^*$), and that
   distinction is the core of the argument.
4. **"Taylor expanding $-\log g(\hat x)$ around $x_0$."** The expression
   that follows has $-\log g(\hat x)$ as its constant term, which is an
   expansion *around* $\hat x$ (our Half 2), not around $x_0$ (our
   Half 1). The quadratic term also has a bare $x$ where $x_0$ is meant.
5. **"the likelihood is flat at $\hat x$."** True for the observed
   likelihood (Half 2). In Half 1 the reason is different: the
   *expected* NLL is flat at $\theta_0$.
6. **Calling $V$ "the information matrix."** $V$ is the Hessian of the
   log-likelihood, which is the *negative* of the information. His next
   statement, $-V^{-1} \approx \Sigma$, is correct.
7. **"By definition, $E[(x - \hat x)^T(x - \hat x)]$ also equals $\Sigma$."**
   That's the inner product, a single number. The covariance matrix is
   the outer product, $E[\Delta\Delta^T]$, and it equals $\Sigma$ only
   approximately. The step that connects it to the quadratic form
   $\Delta^T V\Delta$ is the trace trick (Section 3), which the footnote
   skips ("after more math").
8. **The missing factor of 2.** His expansion carries a $\tfrac12$, so
   its expectation is $\tfrac12\,\text{tr}(\Sigma^{-1}\Sigma) = k/2$, not
   $k$. Doubling $\text{NLL} + k/2$ would give a penalty of $k$. The
   footnote reaches $+k$ by dropping the $\tfrac12$. The real
   source of the other $k/2$ is the second expansion: one expansion
   handles Half 2 (in-sample optimism), and Half 1 (the out-of-sample
   cost of estimating $\theta$) is never derived.

Burnham and Anderson (2002, Chapter 7) give the full derivation, in
more general form (including TIC), if you want to check these notes
against a primary source.

# Summary

| Step | What it says | Size |
|:------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:-----------|
| Target | expected NLL of the fitted model on **new** data, $E_y[Q(\hat\theta)]$ | |
| Half 1 | fitted model vs. best model, judged on new data | $+k/2$ |
| Half 2 | best model on its own data vs. fitted model on its own data | $+k/2$ |
| Key tool | $E[\Delta^T A\Delta] = \text{tr}(A\Sigma)$, with $\Sigma \approx \mathcal{I}^{-1}$ | $\text{tr}(I_k) = k$ |
| AIC | $2\,[\text{NLL}_y(\hat\theta) + k]$ | $-2\log\mathcal{L} + 2k$ |

In one sentence: **a model fitted and scored on the same data looks
better than it is by about $k$ NLL units, half because the fitted
parameters miss the best ones and half because they chase the noise in
the data they were fitted to, and AIC adds that $k$ back (doubled).**
